title: Hola and Hasta Luego
bigQuestion: How does the way you say hello and goodbye show respect for the person in front of you?

story.title: First Day in Pilsen
story.kicker: A new seventh grader learns that one hello does not fit every person.
paragraphs: Daniela walked into her new middle school in Pilsen, a Chicago neighborhood where many families have roots in Mexico. It was eight in the morning. A woman at the front desk smiled and said, "Buenos días" (good morning). Daniela answered, "Buenos días," and felt a little braver.

In the hallway, a boy with a soccer ball under his arm waved at her. "¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?" he said (Hi! How's it going?). Daniela laughed. "Bien, ¿y tú?" (Good, and you?). His name was Tomás. He pointed down the hall and said, "Vamos, la clase es allí" (Come on, the class is there).

Before class, Tomás stopped next to a tall man with gray hair. "Señor Ramírez, le presento a Daniela," he said (Mr. Ramírez, let me introduce Daniela to you). The teacher shook her hand. "Mucho gusto, Daniela" (Nice to meet you). Daniela noticed that Tomás used a more formal way to talk to the teacher than he used with her.

At three o'clock, the bell rang. Tomás gave her a quick wave. "¡Chao, Daniela! ¡Hasta mañana!" (Bye, Daniela! See you tomorrow!). At the door, Daniela turned to Señor Ramírez. "Hasta luego, señor" (See you later, sir). He smiled. "Hasta luego, Daniela. Buenas tardes" (Good afternoon).
story.think: Tomás talked one way to Daniela and another way to Señor Ramírez. Why do you think he changed how he spoke?

lessons.title: Buenos Días
lessons.mainIdea: Say buenos días (good morning) from when you wake up until about noon.
reading: Picture walking into school at eight in the morning. The office worker looks up. In Spanish, the polite hello at this hour is *buenos días* (good morning). It literally means "good days," in the plural. English speakers often say "buen día" or "bueno día" by mistake. Many people say buen día in some countries, but buenos días is the standard greeting everywhere.

Look at the pieces. Buenos is an adjective, a word that describes a noun. Días is a noun, a word for a thing. Día (day) is a masculine noun even though it ends in -a. So the adjective takes the masculine plural ending -os: buenos días. You will meet this odd noun again: el día (the day).

Use buenos días with anyone: a teacher, a bus driver, a friend's grandmother. It works from waking up until lunch time, around noon. You can add a name or a title: "Buenos días, señora López" (Good morning, Mrs. López). The word *señora* (ma'am, Mrs.) shows respect.

words.d: good morning — the greeting from waking up until about noon
the day — a masculine noun that ends in -a
ma'am, Mrs. — a respectful title for a woman: Buenos días, señora

look.title: Which Greeting When? (Example Times)
look.cite: Example times; the switch from tardes to noches often comes when it gets dark, and customs vary by country
look.prompt: At 10:00 a.m. you meet your principal. Which greeting fits, and why?

check.q: It is 9:00 a.m. You walk into the school office. What do you say?
check.why: Buenos días is the morning greeting. Día is masculine, so the adjective is buenos, not buenas.

check.q: Why is it buenos días and not buenas días?
choices: Because día is a masculine noun, even though it ends in -a.
Because buenas is only for plural words.
check.why: El día is one of the few masculine nouns ending in -a, so its adjective uses -os.

check.q: Which greeting shows respect to an older woman in the morning?
check.why: Buenos días is the morning hello, and señora is a respectful title.

lessons.title: Buenas Tardes and Buenas Noches
lessons.mainIdea: Say buenas tardes in the afternoon and buenas noches at night, both as hello and as goodbye.
reading: Picture yourself arriving at your aunt's house at four in the afternoon. The greeting now is *buenas tardes* (good afternoon). La tarde (the afternoon) is a feminine noun, so the adjective is buenas, with -as. Many people use buenas tardes from lunch until it gets dark, so early evening can still be tarde.

When it is dark, the greeting becomes *buenas noches* (good evening, good night). La noche (the night) is also feminine, so it is buenas noches. English has two phrases here, good evening and good night, but Spanish uses one. That means buenas noches works when you arrive at a party at nine and when you go to bed.

Watch the pattern: buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches. Only the first one uses -os, because only día is masculine. A common mistake is to copy the first one and say "buenos tardes." Check the noun first, then choose the ending. In quick, casual speech, some people just say "¡Buenas!" for any of these.

words.d: good afternoon — from about noon until dark; also used as goodbye
good evening or good night — used after dark, as hello or goodbye
the night — a feminine noun, so buenas noches

look.title: One Day, Three Greetings
look.text:
7:30 a.m., at the bus stop: "Buenos días, señor."
3:00 p.m., at the corner store: "Buenas tardes, señora."
8:30 p.m., arriving at a cousin's party: "Buenas noches, tía." (tía = aunt)
11:00 p.m., going to bed: "Buenas noches, mamá."
look.prompt: Write your own day with three greetings. Pick a time, a place and a person for each one.

check.q: It is 3:00 p.m. What is the right greeting?
check.why: Buenas tardes is the afternoon greeting. Tarde is feminine, so it takes buenas.

check.q: You are leaving a friend's house at 10:00 p.m. What can you say?
check.why: Buenas noches works as a goodbye at night, and noche is feminine.

check.q: Which greeting is the only one of the three that uses -os?
check.why: Only día is masculine, so only buenos días uses -os.

lessons.title: Hola and ¿Qué Tal?
lessons.mainIdea: Hola is a friendly hi for any time of day, and ¿Qué tal? asks how things are going.
reading: Picture seeing your best friend in the lunch line. You do not need to check the clock. You just say *hola* (hi, hello). The h in hola is silent, so it sounds like "OH-lah." English speakers often pronounce the h, but in Spanish the letter h makes no sound.

Friends often add a quick question: *¿Qué tal?* (How's it going? What's up?). Notice the upside-down question mark ¿ at the start. Spanish marks the beginning and the end of every question. Qué has an accent mark because it is a question word here.

Hola is friendly and works with almost everyone. With an adult you do not know well, pair it with a time greeting: "Hola, buenos días." That sounds warm and polite at the same time. A fast answer to ¿Qué tal? is "Bien, ¿y tú?" (Good, and you?).

words.d: hi, hello — works any time of day; the h is silent
How's it going? — a friendly, casual question after hola

look.title: Lunch Line Hello
look.text:
Ana: ¡Hola, Marco! ¿Qué tal?
Marco: Bien, ¿y tú?
Ana: Muy bien, gracias.
(Hi, Marco! How's it going? / Good, and you? / Very good, thanks.)
Notice: ¡ opens the exclamation, ¿ opens the question, and the h in hola stays silent.
look.prompt: Act out this dialogue with a partner. Then change it so one person is tired and answers differently.

check.q: How do you pronounce hola?
choices: oh-LAH, with the stress at the end
check.why: The Spanish h is silent, and the stress falls on the first syllable: OH-lah.

check.q: Which is written correctly?
check.why: A Spanish question opens with ¿ and closes with ?, and qué has an accent as a question word.

check.q: Your friend says, "¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?" What is a good answer?
check.why: ¿Qué tal? asks how it's going, so you answer with how you are: Bien, ¿y tú?

lessons.title: Answering ¿Cómo Estás?
lessons.mainIdea: Answer ¿Cómo estás? with bien, muy bien, más o menos or mal, and ask back with ¿y tú?
reading: Picture your cousin calling you after a long test day. She asks, "¿Cómo estás?" (How are you?). This question asks how you feel right now. The answer starts with a word for your mood, and you can add "gracias" (thanks) to be polite.

Here is a scale from best to worst. *Muy bien* means very well. *Bien* means well or fine. *Más o menos* means so-so, literally "more or less." Mal means bad or not well. A full answer can use estoy (I am): "Estoy bien." You can also say just "Bien, gracias."

Do not stop there. Ask back: "¿Y tú?" (And you?) to a friend. English speakers sometimes answer "Bien" and then walk away, which can sound cold. Another mistake is to say "Soy bien." For how you feel, Spanish uses estoy, not soy. You will study that difference in a later unit.

words.d: How are you? — asks a friend how they feel right now
well, fine — Estoy bien (I'm fine); muy bien means very well
so-so — literally more or less
bad, not well — Estoy mal (I'm not doing well)

look.title: Four Answers
look.text:
¿Cómo estás?
After a great game: "¡Muy bien, gracias!"
On a normal day: "Bien, ¿y tú?"
With a small headache: "Más o menos."
With a bad cold: "Estoy mal."
Each answer names the feeling first, then can add gracias or ¿y tú?
look.prompt: How are you today? Answer in Spanish with one of the four words and ask a partner back.

check.q: What does "Más o menos" mean as an answer to ¿Cómo estás?
check.why: Más o menos literally means more or less and is used for so-so.

check.q: Which answer is correct Spanish for "I'm fine"?
check.why: For how you feel, Spanish uses estoy (I am): Estoy bien.

check.q: Your friend says, "Muy bien, ¿y tú?" What is she doing?
choices: Saying she is very well and asking how you are
check.why: Muy bien means very well, and ¿y tú? means and you?

lessons.title: Adiós and Hasta Luego
lessons.mainIdea: Adiós means goodbye, and hasta luego means see you later.
reading: Picture the bell ringing at the end of the day. You leave the classroom. The simplest goodbye is *adiós* (goodbye). It has a written accent on the o: adiós. Without the accent, the word is spelled wrong. The stress falls on the last syllable, "ah-DYOHS."

Many people prefer *hasta luego* (see you later). Hasta means until, and luego means later, so it is literally "until later." It sounds friendly because it expects to see the person again. You can say it to a teacher, a store clerk or a friend.

Some English speakers think adiós means goodbye forever. It does not. People say adiós every day. Still, hasta luego is very common when you will see someone soon. You can even use both: "Adiós, hasta luego." Remember that the h in hasta is silent: "AHS-tah LWEH-go."

words.d: goodbye — always written with an accent on the o
see you later — literally until later
until — the start of many goodbyes: hasta luego, hasta mañana

look.title: Leaving the Store
look.text:
Cashier: Aquí tiene. (Here you go.)
Luis: Gracias. Adiós.
Cashier: Hasta luego.
Luis says a simple goodbye. The cashier answers with see you later, a friendly way to expect him back.
look.prompt: You leave a taquería after lunch. Write a two-line goodbye between you and the cook.

check.q: What does hasta luego mean?
check.why: Hasta means until and luego means later: see you later.

check.q: Which spelling is correct?
check.why: Adiós carries a written accent that slants up to the right, on the o.

check.q: Does adiós only mean goodbye forever?
choices: Yes, never use it at school.
Yes, it is only for funerals.
No, people say it every day.
check.why: Adiós is an everyday goodbye; English speakers sometimes wrongly think it is final.

lessons.title: Hasta Mañana and Chao
lessons.mainIdea: Hasta mañana means see you tomorrow, and chao is a casual bye among friends.
reading: Picture Friday afternoon versus Thursday afternoon. On Thursday, you know you will see your friends the next day. So you say *hasta mañana* (see you tomorrow). Mañana means tomorrow, and it has the letter ñ. The ñ sounds like the ny in canyon: "mah-NYAH-nah."

Among friends, many people say *chao* (bye). It comes from the Italian word ciao, and it is common in much of Latin America. Some people spell it chau. Use chao with friends and family, not in a formal moment, like leaving a job interview.

Here is the pattern: hasta + a time word. Hasta luego is until later. Hasta mañana is until tomorrow. A mistake English speakers make is writing manana without the tilde. Without the ñ, the word is misspelled, and the sound changes. Always type ñ.

words.d: see you tomorrow — mañana means tomorrow and uses ñ
bye — casual, used with friends and family
tomorrow — also means morning when used as la mañana

look.title: Thursday at 3:00
look.text:
Sofía: ¡Chao, Tomás! ¡Hasta mañana!
Tomás: ¡Chao! Hasta mañana.
Sofía: (to the teacher) Hasta mañana, profesora.
She uses chao with Tomás but not with the teacher. Hasta mañana works for both.
look.prompt: Why does Sofía skip chao with her teacher? Write one goodbye for a friend and one for a teacher.

check.q: It is Tuesday. You will see your friend at school on Wednesday. What fits best?
check.why: Hasta mañana means see you tomorrow.

check.q: When is chao a poor choice?
choices: Ending a call with a friend
check.why: Chao is casual. A formal moment calls for adiós, hasta luego or buenas tardes.

check.q: How is the ñ in mañana pronounced?
check.why: Ñ sounds like the ny in canyon: mah-NYAH-nah.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Goodbye
lessons.mainIdea: Pick a goodbye by asking when you will meet again and how close you are to the person.
reading: Picture three people you say goodbye to on one day: your little brother, the school nurse and a new friend from art class. Each goodbye can fit a different situation. Two questions help you pick. When will I see this person again? How formal is this moment?

If you will meet tomorrow, say hasta mañana. If you will meet later today or soon, say hasta luego. If you do not know, adiós always works. At night, buenas noches can also mean goodbye. With friends and family, chao is quick and warm.

Many speakers also say *nos vemos* (see you, literally we see each other). It is friendly and fits most people you know. A common learner mistake is to say "buenos días" when leaving in the morning. Some people do use it that way, but hasta luego is clearer for goodbye.

words.d: see you — literally we see each other; friendly goodbye
goodbye — the safe choice for anyone, any time

look.title: Three Goodbyes
look.text:
To your little brother at the bus stop: "¡Chao! Nos vemos."
To the school nurse at 2:00 p.m.: "Gracias. Buenas tardes."
To a new friend on Monday, who has art again on Tuesday: "¡Hasta mañana!"
look.prompt: Choose a goodbye for your coach after practice on Friday, when you meet again on Monday. Explain your choice.

check.q: You will not see your friend again until next week. Which goodbye does NOT fit?
check.why: Hasta mañana means see you tomorrow, which is not true here.

check.q: What does nos vemos mean?
check.why: Nos vemos literally means we see each other and is used like see you.

check.q: You leave a doctor's office at 4:00 p.m. What is a polite goodbye?
check.why: Buenas tardes works as a goodbye in the afternoon, and it is polite enough for a doctor.

lessons.title: Tú Versus Usted
lessons.mainIdea: Use tú with friends, family and kids, and usted with adults you should show respect to.
reading: Picture Tomás talking to Daniela and then to his teacher. English has one word for you. Spanish has two for one person. *Tú* (you) is informal, used with friends, classmates, family and children. *Usted* (you) is formal, used with a teacher, a principal, a doctor or an older stranger.

The verb changes too. With tú, the verb usually ends in -s: "¿Cómo estás?" With usted, the verb matches él and ella: "¿Cómo está usted?" So estás goes with tú, and está goes with usted. Listen for that final -s to know which one someone used.

Customs differ. In some families, kids use usted with their own parents or grandparents. In other places, almost everyone uses tú. When you are not sure, start with usted. If the person says "Háblame de tú" (talk to me with tú), you can switch. Tú has an accent; tu without an accent means your.

words.d: you (informal) — for friends, family, kids; verb often ends in -s: estás
you (formal) — for teachers, older adults, strangers; ¿Cómo está usted?
polite and respectful in form — the style you use with usted

look.title: Same Question, Two Ways
look.text:
To a classmate: "Hola, Daniela. ¿Cómo estás?"
To the principal: "Buenos días, señora Ortiz. ¿Cómo está usted?"
The question is the same: How are you? The verb changes from estás (tú) to está (usted), and the greeting gets more formal.
look.prompt: Ask your grandmother and your best friend how they are. Write each question and underline the verb.

check.q: You meet your friend's grandfather for the first time. Which question fits?
check.why: With an older adult you just met, use usted, and usted takes está.

check.q: Which verb goes with tú?
check.why: The tú form usually ends in -s: estás.

check.q: What is the difference between tú and tu?
choices: Tu means you; tú means your.
Tú is formal; tu is informal.
Tú means you; tu means your.
check.why: The accent separates the two words: tú (you) and tu (your).

lessons.title: Handshakes and Cheek Kisses
lessons.mainIdea: Many Spanish speakers greet with a touch: a handshake, a hug or a light kiss on the cheek.
reading: Picture arriving at a family party. Your cousin's friends lean in and touch your cheek. In many Spanish-speaking places, people greet with *un beso* (a kiss) on the cheek. It is usually a light touch of cheeks with a kissing sound, not a real kiss. In much of Latin America it is one cheek, and in Spain it is usually two.

In school or business, a firm handshake is common, especially between people who just met. Close friends and family often hug, called *un abrazo* (a hug). Many people greet everyone in the room when they arrive and say goodbye to each person when they leave.

Customs change by country, family and age. Some people prefer not to be touched at all, and that is fine. Watch what others do, and follow the other person's lead. A smile and a clear "Mucho gusto" (nice to meet you) are always welcome.

words.d: the kiss — un beso en la mejilla is a light cheek kiss used as a greeting in many places
the hug — a common greeting between family and close friends
the hand — dar la mano means to shake hands; a feminine noun ending in -o

look.title: Arriving at a Party
look.text: Picture a birthday party in Humboldt Park. You walk in. Your aunt hugs you: un abrazo. Her friend leans in for one cheek kiss: "¡Hola, mi amor!" Your cousin's new neighbor shakes your hand: "Mucho gusto." Before you eat, you greet each person in the room.
look.prompt: How do people greet each other in your family? Compare it with the scene above.

check.q: What is un abrazo?
check.why: Un abrazo means a hug.

check.q: Which statement matches the reading?
choices: Every Spanish speaker greets with two kisses.
In much of Latin America the cheek kiss is on one cheek; in Spain, usually two.
Greeting customs are the same in every country.
check.why: The reading says one cheek is common in much of Latin America and two in Spain, and customs vary.

check.q: You are not sure how to greet someone. What does the reading advise?
check.why: Customs vary, so watch and follow the other person's lead.

lessons.title: Te Presento a… and Mucho Gusto
lessons.mainIdea: Introduce someone with te presento a (informal) or le presento a (formal), and answer mucho gusto.
reading: Picture introducing your new friend Daniela to your cousin. You say, "Te presento a Daniela" (Let me introduce Daniela to you). The phrase *te presento a* is the tú way. Te means to you, informal. The little word a comes before a person's name, so do not drop it.
To introduce someone to a teacher, switch to the usted way: "Le presento a Daniela." Le means to you, formal. The rest stays the same. This is the same choice as tú versus usted, now inside a phrase.

The new people answer *mucho gusto* (nice to meet you, literally much pleasure). The other person can say "Igualmente" (likewise) or "El gusto es mío" (the pleasure is mine). A mistake English speakers make is saying "Mucho gusto" to someone they already know. It is only for a first meeting.

words.d: let me introduce … to you (informal): Te presento a Ana
let me introduce … to you (formal, usted): Le presento a mi mamá
nice to meet you — said at a first meeting
likewise — a reply to mucho gusto

look.title: Three People Meet
look.text:
Tomás: Daniela, te presento a mi primo Leo. (my cousin)
Leo: Mucho gusto, Daniela.
Daniela: Igualmente.
Tomás: Señor Ramírez, le presento a Leo.
Sr. Ramírez: Mucho gusto, Leo.
Leo: El gusto es mío.
look.prompt: Introduce a friend to your coach, then to your sister. Which words change, and why?

check.q: You introduce your friend to your principal. What do you say?
check.why: With a principal you use the formal le presento a, and a comes before the name.

check.q: Someone says "Mucho gusto" to you. What is a good reply?
check.why: Igualmente means likewise, a common reply to mucho gusto.

check.q: When is mucho gusto a mistake?
choices: Greeting your best friend of five years
Meeting your friend's mother for the first time
check.why: Mucho gusto is for a first meeting, not for someone you already know.

review.q: It is 8:00 p.m. and dark. You arrive at a party. Which greeting fits?
review.why: After dark, buenas noches is both hello and goodbye, and noche is feminine.

review.q: Which pair uses tú and usted correctly?
review.why: Use tú (estás) with a friend and usted (está) with a teacher.
Mañana means tomorrow, so hasta mañana is see you tomorrow.

review.q: Daniela says, "Profesor, le presento a mi mamá." What is she doing?
choices: Introducing her mom to her teacher, formally
Introducing her teacher to her friend, informally
review.why: Le presento a is the formal way to introduce someone.

review.q: Which word has a silent letter?
review.why: The h in hola is silent in Spanish.

review.q: A friend asks, "¿Qué tal?" You had a so-so day. What do you answer?
review.why: Más o menos means so-so, and it answers a how-are-you question.

review.q: Which goodbye is too casual for a job interview?
review.why: Chao is casual, used with friends and family.

review.q: Which statement about greeting customs is accurate?
choices: Everyone who speaks Spanish kisses two cheeks.
Customs vary by country, family and person.
Only children kiss on the cheek.
review.why: Greeting customs differ from place to place and person to person.
